cards.front: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
cards.back: Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once; parallelism is doing many at the same instant
cards.extra: A single-core CPU can be concurrent (interleaved) but not parallel. Parallelism needs several cores.

cards.back: The maximum speedup from parallelising a task, limited by its serial fraction
cards.extra: If 20% of the work cannot be parallelised, no number of cores gets you past 5×. The serial part dominates.

cards.back: The result depends on the timing of thread interleavings inside a critical section
cards.extra: Same input, different output, depending on scheduling. It may pass a thousand runs and fail in production.

cards.back: Code that must not be executed by two threads at the same time
cards.extra: Identified by shared mutable state plus read-modify-write. It is what you must guard.

cards.front: What are the four conditions for deadlock?
cards.back: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait
cards.extra: Break any one and deadlock is impossible. The book's usual advice: enforce lock ordering to kill circular wait.

cards.front: What is lock ordering, and why does it prevent deadlock?
cards.back: Every thread acquires locks in the same defined order, so no cycle can form
cards.extra: Without a global order, thread A waits for B's lock while B waits for A's.

cards.back: A thread never gets CPU or a lock because others always win the contention
cards.extra: Priority misuse and unfair locks cause it. Fairness settings trade throughput for guaranteed progress.

cards.back: Two threads writing different variables that sit on the same cache line, so the line bounces between cores
cards.extra: The variables are independent, but the hardware invalidates the whole line. Padding fields apart can help.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model

cards.back: That writes before it are visible to reads after it, in a defined order
cards.extra: It is the formal rule behind synchronized, volatile and thread start/join. Without it, visibility is undefined.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model

cards.front: What is the Java Memory Model, in one sentence?
cards.back: The rules that say when a write by one thread becomes visible to another
cards.extra: It allows each thread its own working copy of shared variables; happens-before is what forces a refresh.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model

cards.front: Why does volatile exist, given the JMM?
cards.back: It forces reads and writes to go to main memory, giving visibility without locking
cards.extra: It does not make i++ atomic — it only fixes visibility and ordering, not compound operations.

cards.back: A thread that already holds the lock can acquire it again
cards.extra: Java's synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant; a naive spin lock is not, and self-deadlocks.

cards.back: A thread checks a condition, another thread changes it, and the first acts on the stale check
cards.extra: The check and the action must be inside the same lock; otherwise the gap is the bug.

cards.back: Each thread holds one lock and waits for the other's, with no circular dependency to break by ordering
cards.extra: It looks like deadlock but is a different failure: the wait/notify is inside a monitor that the other thread needs.

cards.back: Per-thread storage: each thread sees its own value of the variable
cards.extra: The classic use is non-thread-safe objects reused per thread (formatters, connections). It leaks if threads are pooled and never cleared.

cards.front: What is a thread pool for?
cards.back: Reusing threads to run tasks, so thread creation is not paid per task
cards.extra: Bounded worker count also protects the system from unbounded concurrency.

cards.back: Many threads competing for the same lock, so most of the time is spent waiting and context-switching
cards.extra: Throughput collapses even though nothing is broken. Fix by reducing the critical section or partitioning the state.

cards.back: Producers put items into a queue; consumers take them out, decoupling the two rates
cards.extra: The queue is the synchronisation point: bound it and producers block when the consumer is slow.

cards.front: What is the difference between ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue?
cards.back: Array-backed with a fixed capacity versus linked nodes with optional capacity
cards.extra: The array version is bounded by construction; the linked one defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE, which is effectively unbounded.

cards.back: A queue with no capacity: each put must wait for a matching take
cards.extra: It is a handoff, not a buffer — used by cached thread pools to pass a task straight to a waiting worker.

cards.back: A counter limiting how many threads may hold a permit at once
cards.extra: Acquire before the resource, release after. With 1 permit it behaves like a mutex.

cards.back: Waiting until N events have happened: each countDown() decrements, await() returns at zero
cards.extra: One-shot: it cannot be reset. Use it to wait for startup tasks to finish.

cards.back: Making N threads wait for each other at a point, then continue together — and it can be reused
cards.extra: The reusable counterpart to CountDownLatch: rounds of work that must synchronise between phases.

cards.back: A rendezvous point where two threads swap objects
cards.extra: Both block until both arrive, then exchange — a two-party handoff with no queue.

cards.front: What do the Atomic* classes give you?
cards.back: Lock-free read-modify-write operations such as incrementAndGet and compareAndSet
cards.extra: They use CAS under the hood, so they scale better than a lock when contention is low.

cards.back: An atomic instruction: "set to new if still equal to expected", returning whether it worked
cards.extra: The basis of lock-free algorithms. On failure you retry — hence the loop in every CAS-based method.

cards.front: What is the difference between Callable and Runnable?
cards.back: Callable returns a value and may throw checked exceptions; Runnable does neither
cards.extra: A Callable submitted to an executor gives you a Future to collect the result.

cards.back: The result of an asynchronous computation — get() blocks until it is ready
cards.extra: get() also rethrows the task's exception, wrapped in ExecutionException.

cards.back: Divide-and-conquer work that splits into subtasks and steals them from other workers' queues
cards.extra: It shines for recursive, CPU-bound tasks with uneven subproblem sizes; parallel streams use it by default.

cards.front: What does ReadWriteLock allow that a plain lock does not?
cards.back: Many readers at once, or one writer alone
cards.extra: Good for read-heavy state. Watch for writer starvation if readers arrive continuously.

cards.front: What is the trade-off of virtual threads?
cards.back: Cheap blocking (millions of them), but no benefit for CPU-bound work
cards.extra: They let a thread-per-request style scale, because blocking parks a virtual thread instead of an OS thread.

cards.back: Runs a task repeatedly at a fixed rate from the start of each run
cards.extra: Fixed rate means a slow run can bunch up; scheduleWithFixedDelay waits between runs instead.

cards.front: What is the difference between ConcurrentMap and a plain Map under concurrency?
cards.back: It defines atomic operations — putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, replace, merge
cards.extra: A synchronized Map makes each call safe but not a check-then-act sequence. These methods are the sequence.
